questions.question: How do you implement caching in Spring Boot using the @Cacheable and @CacheEvict annotations with Redis?
questions.title: Spring Cache Abstraction with Redis (@Cacheable, @CacheEvict)
questions.direct_answer: Spring's cache abstraction lets you declaratively add Redis caching to any Spring bean method using @Cacheable to cache results, @CachePut to update the cache, and @CacheEvict to invalidate entries — all without mixing caching logic into business code. You configure a RedisCacheManager bean to connect Spring's abstraction to Redis, set TTLs per cache, and choose a serializer. The result is clean service code where caching is a cross-cutting concern managed by AOP proxies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of wiring Spring caching to Redis, including configuration, key generation, and cache eviction strategies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to add @EnableCaching on the configuration class, or not configuring a custom KeyGenerator, leading to key collisions between methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the proxy-based limitation (self-invocation doesn't hit the cache), custom key expressions with SpEL, and how to configure per-cache TTLs.

sections.title: How it works under the hood
sections.content:
Spring's cache abstraction decouples caching logic from business code using an AOP proxy model. When the application context starts, Spring scans for `@Cacheable`, `@CachePut`, and `@CacheEvict` annotations and wraps the annotated beans in a proxy. On every call to a `@Cacheable` method, the proxy intercepts the invocation, computes the cache key from the method arguments (using SpEL if specified), and checks the configured `CacheManager`. If the key exists, the cached value is returned without invoking the target method. On a miss, the method executes, and the return value is stored in the cache for future calls.

The `RedisCacheManager` bridges Spring's abstraction to Redis. Under the hood it uses `RedisTemplate` to serialize keys and values, store them as Redis Strings with an optional TTL, and prefix every key with the cache name to avoid collisions across different `@Cacheable` targets. Configuring per-cache TTLs is critical in production: a user-profile cache might tolerate 30 minutes of staleness, while a pricing cache might need a 60-second TTL to stay fresh during promotions.

The most common pitfall is the proxy-based self-invocation trap. Because Spring intercepts calls at the proxy boundary, a method calling another `@Cacheable` method on `this` bypasses the cache entirely — the call never passes through the proxy. The fix is to inject a self-reference or extract the cached method into a separate bean. Another subtlety is key collisions: if two different methods share the same cache name and happen to receive identical arguments, their entries collide. Using explicit `key` expressions with `#root.methodName` or a custom `KeyGenerator` prevents this. Finally, `@Cacheable(sync = true)` tells Spring to synchronize cache population for a given key, which mitigates cache stampedes when a hot key expires under high concurrency.

sections.title: Step 1 — Add Dependencies
sections.content:
Add the Redis starter and Spring cache dependencies to your build file:

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
# application.yml — Redis connection
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
      port: 6379
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:}
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 16
          max-idle: 8
```

Spring Boot auto-configures a `LettuceConnectionFactory` from these properties. The Lettuce client is non-blocking and thread-safe, so a single connection factory serves the entire application.

sections.title: Step 2 — Enable Caching and Configure RedisCacheManager
Step 3 — Annotate Service Methods
Step 4 — Conditional Caching and Custom Keys
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Cacheable` skips method execution on cache hit** — first call executes and caches; subsequent calls return cached value; method body is never reached again until the cache expires or is evicted
- **`@CacheEvict` after writes prevents stale reads** — annotate the update and delete methods with eviction; without eviction, the cache returns the old value until the TTL expires
- **`@CachePut` keeps cache warm on writes** — always executes the method and updates the cache; combine with `@CacheEvict` or use instead of it when you want the updated value immediately cached
- **Always configure TTL on caches** — without TTL, Redis entries persist until evicted; a service restart or deployment doesn't clear them; stale data can survive arbitrarily long
- **Cache key collisions cause silent bugs** — if two methods share the same cache name and key expression, one method's cached value is returned for the other; use distinct cache names or key expressions per method

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Spring's cache abstraction lets you add Redis caching to any Spring bean method with three annotations — `@Cacheable`, `@CachePut`, and `@CacheEvict` — without coupling the business logic to the caching implementation.

**`@Cacheable` — cache on first call**
- Place `@Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id")` on a method — on the first call, the method executes and the return value is stored in Redis under the key `products::id`; subsequent calls with the same argument return the cached value without executing the method
- The cache key defaults to the method parameters; use SpEL expressions to compose custom keys: `key = "#user.id + ':' + #status"`

**`@CacheEvict` — invalidate on mutation**
- Place `@CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#id")` on a service method that updates or deletes a product — when that method executes, Spring removes the corresponding Redis key so the next read fetches fresh data
- `allEntries = true` evicts every key in the named cache — useful after a bulk import that invalidates everything

**`@CachePut` — update the cache on write**
- `@CachePut` always executes the method AND updates the cache — unlike `@Cacheable` which skips the method on a hit; use it on create or update methods to keep the cache warm

**Configuration in Spring Boot**
- Add `spring-boot-starter-data-redis` and configure `spring.redis.host`; add `@EnableCaching` to the application; Spring Boot auto-configures a `RedisCacheManager` using Jackson for serialization
- Configure TTL per cache: `RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig().entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10))` — without TTL, cached values live until evicted, which can cause stale data to persist indefinitely

questions.question: How do you configure Spring Session with Redis to enable distributed session storage in a multi-instance Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Spring Session + Redis for Distributed Session Storage
questions.direct_answer: Spring Session replaces the default in-memory HttpSession with a Redis-backed session store, enabling any application instance to serve any request regardless of which instance created the session. You add spring-session-data-redis to your dependencies, annotate a configuration class with @EnableRedisHttpSession, and configure a Redis connection — Spring's autoconfiguration handles the rest. Session data is stored as a Redis Hash, and the session ID is passed via a cookie or HTTP header.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the stateless application pattern, sticky session problems, and how Redis-backed sessions enable horizontal scaling.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Spring Session without setting appropriate session timeouts, leading to Redis being filled with abandoned sessions that consume significant memory.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the difference between cookie-based and header-based session ID propagation, discuss session data serialization concerns, and explain how Spring Session supports multiple session repositories (Redis, JDBC, Hazelcast).

sections.title: How it works under the hood
sections.content:
HTTP session management becomes a distributed systems problem the moment you scale beyond a single application instance. With in-memory sessions, each JVM holds its own session map, so the load balancer must route every request from a given user to the same instance (sticky sessions). This creates uneven load distribution, complicates rolling deployments, and means a single instance failure loses all its active sessions.

Spring Session solves this by replacing the servlet container's default `HttpSession` implementation with a pluggable `SessionRepository`. The Redis implementation stores each session as a Redis Hash under a namespaced key (e.g., `spring:session:sessions:<uuid>`), with each session attribute serialized as a Hash field. A separate Redis key with an expiry tracks the session's max inactive interval, and Spring Session uses Redis keyspace notifications to detect expired sessions and fire `SessionDestroyedEvent` to application listeners.

The flush mode setting controls write timing. `ON_SAVE` (default) buffers attribute changes in memory and flushes to Redis only when the HTTP response is committed — this batches writes and reduces Redis round-trips but risks data loss if the JVM crashes mid-request. `IMMEDIATE` mode writes every `setAttribute` call to Redis synchronously, which is safer for long-running requests or WebSocket connections where the response is never formally committed.

Serialization deserves attention: every object stored in the session must be serializable. JDK serialization works out of the box but produces verbose payloads and is fragile across class version changes. Switching to JSON serialization (via Jackson) produces human-readable Redis entries and avoids `ClassNotFoundException` during rolling deployments, but requires careful handling of polymorphic types. Keep session payloads small — large session objects inflate Redis memory and add latency to every request that touches the session.

sections.title: Step 1 — Add Dependencies
sections.content:
Add Spring Session and Redis dependencies:

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

Spring Boot auto-configures Spring Session when it detects the `spring-session-data-redis` dependency on the classpath. No additional code is needed for the basic setup.

sections.title: Step 2 — Enable Redis HTTP Session
Step 3 — Configure Redis and Session in application.yml
sections.content:
```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost}
      port: ${REDIS_PORT:6379}
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:}
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 16
          max-idle: 8
          min-idle: 2

  session:
    store-type: redis              # Explicitly select Redis
    timeout: 30m                   # Max inactive interval
    redis:
      namespace: myapp:session     # Key prefix
      flush-mode: on-save          # or "immediate" for WebSocket/SSE

server:
  servlet:
    session:
      cookie:
        name: SESSIONID
        http-only: true
        secure: true
        max-age: -1                # Session cookie (expires on browser close)
```

**Redis key structure** created by Spring Session:
- `myapp:session:sessions:<uuid>` — Hash containing session attributes
- `myapp:session:expirations:<timestamp>` — Set of session IDs expiring at that time
- `myapp:session:sessions:expires:<uuid>` — Phantom key for keyspace notification on expiry

sections.title: Step 4 — Use Session Normally
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Session externalizes HTTP sessions to Redis** — any app instance serves any user's request; no sticky sessions required; instance failures don't invalidate sessions
- **Sessions stored as Redis Hashes** — each session attribute is a Hash field under `spring:session:sessions:{id}`; partial attribute reads don't deserialize the entire session object
- **JSON serialization prevents ClassNotFoundException on deployment** — default Java serialization fails if the serialized class changes; configure Jackson-based serialization for deployment compatibility
- **Set session timeout explicitly** — `server.servlet.session.timeout=30m`; without it, sessions default to 30 minutes in Spring Boot; configure to match your application's session lifecycle expectations
- **Monitor Redis latency for sessions** — every authenticated request reads the session from Redis; latency spikes in Redis directly cause latency spikes in all authenticated endpoints; keep Redis on the same network segment

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Spring Session replaces the default in-memory `HttpSession` with a Redis-backed session store, enabling horizontal scaling without sticky sessions.

**The problem it solves**
- By default, Spring Boot stores sessions in application memory — which means if a load balancer routes a user's second request to a different app instance, that instance has no record of the session, and the user appears logged out
- The traditional fix is sticky sessions (session affinity): the load balancer pins each user to one instance; the problem is that instance failures lose all sessions on that node, and load distribution becomes uneven as instances have different session loads
- Spring Session externalizes the session to Redis: every instance reads from and writes to the same Redis store, which means any instance can handle any request for any user

**Configuration in Spring Boot**
- Add `spring-boot-starter-data-redis` and `spring-session-data-redis`; the session store is auto-configured; configure timeout with `server.servlet.session.timeout`
- Spring Session serializes the session to a Redis Hash under `spring:session:sessions:{sessionId}` — each session attribute is a Hash field; reading one attribute doesn't deserialize the entire session

**Session clustering considerations**
- Redis for sessions introduces a network round trip on every request — typically fast (sub-millisecond on the same network), but it's worth measuring; use connection pooling to avoid connection overhead
- `@SessionScope` beans work correctly with Spring Session — the session bean's lifecycle is tied to the Redis-backed session, not the application instance
- Configure session serialization carefully: the default Java serialization can cause ClassNotFoundException after a deployment if serialized classes change; use JSON serialization with a consistent schema
